### THE 1ST BOOK'S 13TH CHAPTER

...in this [process], one must look at the material <note>original: *Zeug*; refers to the raw substance or "stuff" being worked</note> as much as the metal, which is still quite tender and young. This imperfection consists of nine distinct parts, which you must consider well; you must take each one on its own and deal with it as is appropriate, if no harm is to come to the ore or metal.

Firstly, observe closely whether the ore is in a state of rising or falling <note>likely referring to the stage of its natural development or its chemical reactivity</note>; then you can easily assist it by its color and its whole **body** <note>original: *corpore*; the physical mass of the substance</note>. For with such a metal that is rising, you must provide assistance at the **surface-leaf** <term>folio</term> <note>original: *folio*; refers to the "leaf" or the outer surface/veneer of the substance during refinement</note>; but for the falling, you must assist at the **stripping** <term>spolio</term> <note>original: *spolio*; related to the removal or "spoiling" of waste layers</note>, otherwise it will fly away <note>i.e., evaporate or volatilize</note>. For it has not yet been finalized in its proper place and in its workshop, and such metal is of that nature; thus, one should experiment a little and become all the bolder and more encouraged in the subsequent work.

Secondly, you must pay attention to the **nourishment** <note>original: *Speise*; literally "food," referring to the raw minerals or additives</note> which is not yet well "digested" (as I might say); you must help it along toward **digestion** <note>alchemical "digestion" is a process of slow maturation through gentle heat</note>, otherwise the **waste** <note>original: *excrementa*; the impurities cast off by the metal</note> cannot easily be separated from it, which would then be the cause of brittleness <note>original: *Ungeschmeidigkeit*; a lack of malleability</note>.

Thirdly, you must pay close attention to the **flow** <note>original: *Fluß*; both the state of being molten and the "flux" added to help the metal melt</note>, so that you liberate it as you would a raw substance that is itself still liquid; for if one opens both flows completely, it is then difficult to bring them back together again. For dissolving a new, non-fluid material and the **mercury of bodies** <term>☿ corporum</term> <note>original: *☿ corporum*; the "mercury" or essential liquid principle extracted from solid metals</note>, which are already fluid on their own, produces nothing but **dross** <note>original: *Sinter*; fused crust or scale formed during heating</note> and **dust** <note>original: *Gestübe*; fine metallic or charcoal dust</note>.

### Of the Imperfect Metals.

Fourthly, do not forget the hardness, but diligently consider at which degree of rising or falling it is, so that you can give it a fire equal to its **body** <note>original: *corporis*</note>. Direct all your work in part toward these **internal fires** <term>uredines</term> <note>original: *uredines*; literally "blights" or "burnings," referring here to the inherent natural heat or corrosive fire within the substance</note>, and join them with your own fire in the material of the **body** <note>original: *corporis*</note>, so that the **internal fires** might be better strengthened and remain. Thus you may best achieve this work. This cold and hot fire is not known to everyone.

### The 1st Book, 15th Chapter

The ore or metal then takes in the **inhalation** <note>original: *Einwitterung*; the process by which the earth "breathes in" celestial or atmospheric influences.</note> that arises from its internal work, and makes use of it; for one sees that the physical elements cannot penetrate deep into the earth. Because these **weatherings** <note>original: *Witterungen*; in this context, the invisible spiritual "breath" or aura emitted by minerals.</note> are invisible—which one cannot see in their own essence, for a person's breath can be better seen and recognized than a mineral weathering, which must be detected by a [divining] rod—they function hidden from view. 

When a metal "works" <note>Refers to the natural alchemical process of maturation within the rock.</note>, it gives off this breath from itself and also draws it back to itself. The outward breath is the "weathering" that follows; the inward breath, however, is this: for with it, the earth must split open and pull the influence into itself so that it may form a <term>body</term> <note>original: *corpus*; the physical substance of the metal.</note>. To this end, the sun must provide assistance, for where the <term>system</term> <note>original: *Systema*; here meaning the organized structure or constitutional arrangement of the mineral.</note> accompanies the weathering—which must be recognized with great skill—there is the purest earth. According to the testimony of some of the Ancients, it is from this pure earth that humanity was first taken; and such earth possesses much hidden power within it for the subsequent refinement of metals. 

Such "inhalation" serves only this purpose, as you have just heard: that it draws in, swallows, and soaks the "food" <note>The nourishing celestial influence or "astral seed."</note> into the <term>body</term>. For you must not think that it simply leaves it lying in the <term>body</term> once it has been brought inside; rather, it is the <term>retentive force</term> <note>original: *vis retentiva*; the power of a substance to hold onto its vital nutrients or qualities.</note> by which it keeps that which has been soaked up and fed into it steady and firm. 

For this purpose, it prepares the material throughout the entire journey from the place where it receives it from the sun, which then drives everything that is heavy downward. This can be seen in all **sap** <note>original: *Safft*; the vital liquid essence or "mercury" of the metals.</note> that is driven downward in this manner. For this reason, certain stones also glow because they are transparent, such as **carbuncles** <term>carbuncle</term> <note>original: *Carfunckel*; a historical term for any red gemstone that was believed to emit its own light, such as a garnet or ruby.</note>, although among us some wish to consider a high-quality ruby as such, but incorrectly. For one can certainly cleanse such **pyrites** <term>pyrite</term> <note>original: *Pyriten*; iron disulfide, famous for producing sparks when struck, hence the name derived from the Greek word for fire.</note> without loss of the fire or the sparkling fire, and so that it does not consume the stone but only gathers it together; and if one holds a **tinder** <note>original: *Zeug*; any material used to catch a spark.</note> to it, it must ignite. Such fire was also kept buried among the **Jews** and still held to be a holy ignition-fire <note>This refers to a story from 2 Maccabees 1:18-22 in the Apocrypha, where the sacred Temple fire was hidden in a dry cistern and later recovered as a thick liquid (naphtha).</note>. But that art is now entirely gone; the world is no longer worthy of it, though it remains [hidden] to the artists like many other...

### Chapter 18 of the First Book.

A **foil** <note>original: *Folium*</note> is a **shedding** <note>original: *spolium*; refers to a skin or casing that is cast off, like that of a snake.</note>, because it is constantly cast off even as it puts on and raises itself up during its ascent. Miners have almost the same way of speaking about their **lustrous ore** <term>Glanz</term> <note>A term for bright, metallic ores like galena.</note> and **deceptive ore** <term>Blende</term> <note>Sphalerite or similar minerals that "blind" or deceive the miner because they look metallic but were historically difficult to smelt.</note>. It is—to provide a parable—like a fire in the midst of its heat and flame: first there is the **shimmer**, then the **embers**, and the **ashes** <note>original: *Båsel*</note> are the **shedding** <note>original: *spolium*</note>. One might imagine that if they only possessed gold, they could manage all these things, but without this process, it cannot be done. Learn first to **foliate** <note>to apply the foil</note> and **spoliate** <note>to strip or shed the layer</note>; then you can set the metal upon it, but not otherwise. 

Such **shimmer** and **glimmer** are visible once they are set, but the **purification** <term>Låuterung</term> is not seen, much like the **vapors** <term>Witterung</term> <note>In mining, this refers to the "weather" or exhalations of the earth that indicate the presence of ore.</note>. Now, the closer such a glimmer is to the **extraction**, the more it enters into a descending ore and the more poisonous it becomes, until the poison is taken from it by fire and water. Then it joins again with the **seed**, for from the seed comes the shimmer, and from the shimmer comes the glimmer. 

There lies here a fine little art to **tincture** <term>tingiren</term> <note>To transform a metal's properties or color using an alchemical agent.</note> more highly through the shimmer, when one brings it into the glimmer. However, one realization always leads to another; and just as one sees and learns from a **deceptive ore** <note>original: *Blende*</note> and a **lustrous ore** <note>original: *Glanz*</note> that no **choke-damp** <note>original: *Schwaden*; dangerous, suffocating gases in a mine.</note> is present, so too one senses it in this glimmer and shimmer in its **mirrors** <term>speculis</term> and night-lights. To **prepare** <term>præpariren</term> such shimmer and glimmer so that it is quickly deposited and then released again is the greatest feat of all; for it deposits with the highest poison found under the earth, and thus it settles and must be "smelled in" <note>absorbed as a vapor</note>. As for what a great poison the **stillness of Mercury** <term>Mercurii</term> <note>Mercury in its inactive or "resting" state, often associated with hazardous cold or vapors.</note> is, especially under the earth...

### CHAPTER 19.
### OF SOOT AND ASH. <note>original Latin: *DE FULIGINE ET CINERE*</note>

### Of Soot and Ash.

As for the **white soot** of metals, which is a most precious **silver-garment** if only one introduces it into the **mercuries** <note>The "mercuries" refer to the essential fluid or spiritual state of the metal, not necessarily common quicksilver.</note>, it is astonishing that the lowest **corruption of the bodies** <note>The decaying or breaking down of the raw material.</note> of metals produces the highest results, and from the highest, the lowest are formed again. Conversely, that which is most public, and which people think they know and can do, is often the worst and most uncertain—perhaps because they do not know the right way.

# The 1st Book's 19th Chapter.

Now, with the help of the <term>burning agents</term> <note>original Latin: *uredinum*. In alchemy, this refers to corrosive substances or "blasts" of fire used to break down materials.</note>, one must extract the soot from all the **mercuries** <note>The essential spirits or fluid principles of the metals.</note>. Tell me now: which "garment" and which metal yields this best? I must say it is that of **Saturn** <note>The alchemical name for Lead.</note>. For an "earth," when ignited, gives off a smoke; that is, a specific kind of smoke, for the thicker the smoke is, the sootier it is. However, as many books as I have read and as many **laborants** <note>Practical alchemists or laboratory workers.</note> as I have seen, they have not been able to achieve this. Yet you find it in **Saturn**, provided you first convert it into an "earth" <note>A metallic calx or powdered oxide created through heat.</note>. This is the entire foundation: what else would you ignite to turn into ash and soot? There you have both—or rather all three—within: soot, ash, and earth; and the fourth is the "coal" or the color.

But I must report here that common laborers believe that when one speaks of the **mercury of bodies** <note>original: *☿ corporum*</note>, it refers to **prepared metallic mercury** <note>original: *☿ metallum præparirt*</note>, or when speaking of the **salts of bodies** <note>original Latin: *Salibus corporum*</note>, they think it is a salt like our common table salt, and that it must be identical in every way. They think the same of the soot and ash, though there is a vast difference; for wood-ash or stone-ash is a much different thing than the ash and soot of metals in color and form, and much more so in their power and potency. Therefore, in such matters, one must look to the power and the Work itself; from this, the name arises. You cannot talk it into existence, nor argue it, nor work it in; even if you and all those who follow you worked on it for a hundred years, it is not called a "work," but an **After-Work** <note>The process of perfecting or refining what nature has already produced in the earth.</note>. This is also the nature of the ash: for when one works the earth—the metallic earth, I mean—just as nature intends in the Work, the soot flies to the top, and the color remains in the middle,

...and the ash below / and each thing particularly therein. For does not the ash have the **salts**? Do not the colors have the **sulphurs**? Does not the soot have the **mercury**? For just as mercury desires to rise upward, so does the soot. Thus the **tincture** <note>The active, color-giving essence of a substance.</note> settles everywhere like an oil; it creeps in like the **bodies** <note>original: *corpora*; the solid physical forms of the metals.</note> and keeps them beautiful. The miners call all such stuff **mountain ores** <note>original: *Bergarten*; often referring to the gangue or non-valuable rock surrounding the ore.</note>, just as the ignorant call all herbs "grass"; yet with great effort, they also occasionally find something therein, so that they do not work entirely in vain. Such ash of **Saturn** <term>Saturn: Lead</term> is very beautiful to see before it rises higher and is transformed into a **Luna** <term>Luna: Silver</term>; for soon it takes on an **antimony** <note>original: *Spießglaß*; stibnite or antimony sulfide, used in refining.</note>. **Of the Sludge and Lye.**

F

...[just as a person knows how to] manage bread carefully, so nature also manages its waste carefully and brings it forth to the light of day, so that it may be put to good use. In this way, the metal is also recognized as being present in the earth by the sludge <term>Schlich</term> <note>original: *Schlich*; in mining, this refers to the fine, muddy residue or "slimes" left over after ore has been crushed and washed.</note> that nature casts out. This sludge is the rock that nature has sucked dry during its labor and which falls away when it is not filled with metal. Because it also carries a portion of the ore with it, it is rightly called *Schlich*, because it thus slips away <note>The author is making a play on words between the noun *Schlich* and the German verb *schleichen*, meaning "to sneak" or "to slip away."</note> from the work and goes off secretly. 

Wherever such sludge is found, pay close attention, for it breaks off from the material <note>original: *Zeug*; a general term for the "stuff" or substance of the metal.</note> and from the workshop in which the metals <note>original: *metalla*</note> work and perform their duties. Such sludge is a certain indication that metal is present there. It is useful for making all kinds of vessels as one might desire; however, I do not place much importance on the form of the vessel, but rather everything depends on the material itself. 

People take so much trouble to obtain the right material for bricks and cupels <term>Capellen</term> <note>Small, porous bowls used by assayers and alchemists to refine precious metals through a process called cupellation.</note>; they try to achieve this by using burnt bones and vine-ash, but it is all in vain. Instead, prepare this sludge for yourself and dry it well. People often try to prepare the clay with iron filings or shavings, but truly, much good material is spoiled by what is added to it. When you wish to cast something, first test the loam <note>original: *Leimen*; a mixture of clay and sand used for molds and furnace linings.</note> thoroughly, for I have often seen the furnaces melt before the material within them did. This material [the sludge], however, does not melt, but holds firm and is better than glass. Miners <note>original: *Bergleute*</note> hold it dear because of the metal it carries with it. But if I were able to obtain it everywhere for my work, I would [take] the metal that is within it...

## Of Sinter and Exhalations. <note>original: *Sinter und Schwaden*; "Sinter" refers to mineral crusts or scale, while "Schwaden" refers to the dross or vapors released by metals.</note>

The very outermost and final waste of metals is sinter <term>Sinter</term> <note>original: *Sinter*; a crust of mineral deposits often found where water drips or in the cooling of metals.</note>, which is nevertheless very good and harmless. I mean, however, the sinter that the metals <note>original: *metalla*</note> discard themselves through their internal fires <term>Vredines</term> <note>original: *Vredines*; likely a reference to the internal corrosive heat or "blights" that push impurities out of the maturing ore.</note>; then there is the slough <note>original: *exuvium*</note> that the weathering <term>Beywitterung</term> <note>original: *Beywitterung*; the natural process by which minerals mature and react with the air and water within the earth</note> leaves behind, which looks like a sinter. This is a different kind of sinter, similar to that which the smiths and the smelters produce here in the forge; for besides the fact that they are always moving their bodies <note>original: *corpora*</note>, they also purify themselves. For although the lyes <term>Laugen</term> <note>original: *Laugen*; metallic waters or solutions that wash through the earth</note> wash down the minerals <note>original: *mineralia*</note> and colors, the metals nonetheless also purify themselves, as can be seen in the sinter that every metal leaves behind in the fire, which is nevertheless not the same as this natural one. In this sinter, one certainly sees that metal is present; for the sinter of the minerals produced by weathering is indeed tangible, recognizable, and visible, so that every mining expert <term>Berg-Verständiger</term> knows it. But the metallic sinter is also found among the slags <term>Schlacken</term>, though it is unrecognizable, which is why the slags are brittle; otherwise, one could forge them or cast them very densely, as some have occasionally attempted to do, but they were unable to remove this sinter. But beneath the earth, near the metals and also near the lyes, one sometimes finds it quite pure, and it is of all the colors that the metals or ores are, except...

This is called the exhalation <term>Schwaden</term>, which is a very terrible poison; for it kills everything that lives, especially that which breathes.

But here on Earth, these things cannot be separated if there is to be fire elsewhere; and while one exists finely and willingly with the other, they are also contrary to one another if one reverses them.

## Of the Burning-Rod.

Although the practice of dowsing <note>original: *Ruthen gehen*; the use of a diving rod to find water or minerals</note> has fallen into misuse by many people and has thereby become detestable, it is nonetheless a thorough method to search for and investigate **metals** <note>original Latin: *Metalla*</note>, provided it is used naturally and correctly. If this rod is to glow and not shine, burn, or flame, it must have a special <term>Substance</term> <note>original: *Zeug*; refers to the alchemical preparation or coating applied to the wood</note> that absorbs such fire; otherwise, it could not be useful. To this, the substance is applied, just as one applies <term>Pitch-Resin</term> <note>original: *PechHarz*</note> or wax to a torch. This substance, however, must not be made from any fatness—whether of animal, tree, or other...

...thing that is above or on the earth, for such <term>Exhalation</term> <note>original: *Witterung*; the invisible vapors or "scent" emitted by metal ores</note> ignites it, because it is strong; therefore no <margin>lime</margin> tallow, wax, pitch, or resin is suitable, nor any mineral, for such breath would ignite and burn away the very "food" <note>the alchemical essence or substance</note> of the metal itself. Instead, it must be a **lime of the earth**; this quickly catches such heat and burns like a lime up here from the heat and moisture, and thus falls hot from the rod. This lime, having been burned up here by the exhalation, is very useful for many things afterwards.

But this exhalation does not attack the oiliness or bitumen-like quality <note>original: *Bergwaxigkeit*; literally "mountain-waxiness"</note>, for how else could the "food" of the minerals arise, which are formed from it? The miners call it a <term>Spar</term> <note>original: *Spath*; a general term for crystalline minerals like calcite or fluorspar</note>; it is a true mortar or **spar-lime** of the earth. However, it is not attacked beneath the earth because it contains many and great moistures within it. Therefore many people think—and especially the scholars—that it is a subterranean marble; but it is no such thing, for it does not endure in the weather up here, but dries out so that it finally allows itself to be ignited by this exhalation.

The great mountains in **Norway** and in **Sweden**, which are full of spar, attack such ores and smolder them away so that they become completely hollow. This awakens and gives off the evil vapor, which settles and remains lying in one place; it becomes heavy and increases, for more of the evil vapor always joins it.

# Of the 1st Book, Chapter 29

For the **vapor** <term>Dampff</term> is the arrow which the **air** <term>Lufft</term> shoots, and it is either a good or a poisoned ray. For the air itself cannot be poisoned, any more than the heart can suffer sickness <note>The author argues that air is a pure, fundamental element; it merely carries the "poison" like a messenger rather than being transformed into poison itself.</note>; it is only the pestilence or the evil vapor within it that brings the harm. Therefore, not everyone dies, but only those into whom this same evil vapor enters. For we must all live by the air; it is not, nor can it become, evil. Therefore, beware of the vapor, or that same projectile of the air, which does such harm within it; thank God for the air, for you must live by it. 

Those who attribute this same evil vapor to the **stars** <term>Gestirn</term> <note>In early modern science, the "stars" or celestial bodies were believed to govern the movement and quality of minerals and gases deep underground.</note> do not do so wrongly, for they also rule with their light and master such vapors, hindering one another with their paths, and reversing or changing the **weather-influences** <term>Witterungen</term> <note>While *Witterung* usually means weather, here it refers to the specific astrological "influence" or "effluvia" emanating from the planets.</note>. Thus, such vapors become more or less frequent, as happens during **eclipses** <note>original: *Eclipsibus*; Latin for eclipses.</note>. 

For when the weather-influences of the stars cannot govern the lower air, then such shameful and poisonous mists and vapors rise up or grow stronger. Likewise, when the mists and vapors of the "lower stars" <note>This likely refers to terrestrial or subterranean echoes of celestial forces.</note> are also obstructed by the fire- and **stone-deposits** <term>Stein-Sätze</term>, they also create such vapor beneath the earth. And especially this deposit, because it is airy, is very harmful; for it wanders about and causes great blockages where there should be openness.

# CHAPTER XXXI.
# CONCERNING THE METALLIC WHETSTONE <note>original: *De Cote Metallico*</note>,
### or
## Concerning the Stone-Deposit.

<image-desc>Faint pencil sketches in the left margin include a triangle and some illegible cursive markings.</image-desc>

When the air <note>In this context, "air" refers to subterranean vapors or gases.</note> is formed entirely from a piece of pure earth, it eventually becomes a stone. However, there are many kinds of stones, just as there are many substances <term>corpora</term> in the earth—notwithstanding that it is all called "earth." The longer this material lies there, the harder and firmer it becomes. Such a stone can be removed by no other means than fire, which then attacks the earth and finally consumes it; for it is and becomes the structural foundation of the earth <term>Erdfesten</term>, just as the ribs and bones are the foundations of a fish or flesh. These, too, the dear God will finally remove with fire. For this reason, the ancients burned their bodies; for although the flesh soon rots in the earth, the bones remain longer, and their best dissolution <term>Verwesung</term> is fire, in which they become ashes, which is an "earth-ash."

Such a deposit harms the metal, for it does not allow the vital air <term>Witterung</term> <note>The author views metals as living things that require "breath" or atmospheric influence to grow; the "Stone-Deposit" acts as a suffocating barrier.</note> to reach it, without which it cannot be alive; instead, it must withdraw—that is, die off. For nothing can pass through it as it does through the earth, which is permeated by the vital vapors, just as the sun’s rays pass through with their effects. This "air" <note>The solidified vapor forming the stone.</note> is found just as one finds no fish without bones <note>original: *Grad* — an archaic term for fishbones.</note>, for it is the earth’s fortification. When it breaks out here at the surface, it yields good whetstones, grinding stones, or touchstones <note>Stones used to test the purity of gold and silver.</note>; it allows no water

->### Concerning the Stone-Deposit.<-

In it, the vapor tends to remain; it cannot enter or penetrate. However, it contains within itself the accompanying fire, albeit dispersed <note>original: *dispersum*</note>. Therefore, when the mountain spirit <term>Berggeist</term> <note>In early mining lore, this could refer to a literal gnome or, more likely here, a reactive subterranean gas.</note> or "fat" <note>Likely referring to bitumen, petroleum, or oily mineral substances.</note> settles against it, the fire draws it in—for it is the fire's nourishment—and it flares out, consuming it. Afterwards, it vents out to the surface through a hole. Then the stone begins to groan <note>original: *rären*; literally to "roar" or "low" like cattle, here describing the sounds of shifting or cracking rock.</note> and crumble <note>original: *milmern*</note>, and that is its death; this is how one must approach it when one wishes to lift <note>In this context, "lifting" refers to the act of quarrying or removing the stone from the earth.</note> it.

Such hornstone <term>Hornstein</term> <note>A hard, flint-like silicate rock known for its durability.</note> is also a good cement, which is then called mortar <term>Merter</term>, for all buildings that are to be stable near water; for it resists all water and does not let it enter. This is clearly seen in the old ruins of the Colossi, the Pyramids, and the Eichelstein <note>The "Acorn Stone," a reference to the Roman Cenotaph of Drusus in Mainz, Germany.</note> in Mainz. For such a purpose, one truly needs such a mortar, which must not be mixed with sand, but with other waters—with "wine-water," like the Nile, of which Pescennius <note>Pescennius Niger, a Roman usurper who famously told his thirsty soldiers they did not need wine because they had the water of the Nile.</note> said: "You seek wine, and you have the Nile" <note>original: *Vinum quæritis, & Nilum habetis*</note>; or other iron-acidic waters.

The Tower of Babel perished for this reason—not because of the elements, but because bricks do not withstand water. The Pyramids still stand because of their good materials, as do other firm buildings, as the ruins testify, which have fallen due to destruction and tearing down, or have collapsed through earthquakes; which finally lifts this deposit. This, however, is the difference between the stone-deposit <term>Stein-Satz</term> and the stone-meal <term>Stein-Meel</term>: that this stone does not lift when it wishes to become hard—which was previously a very noble stone through which the air could pass—but now it begins to turn into a hornstone. The "meal," however, is when it wishes to dissolve and fall <insert>apart</insert> <note>The text continues on the next page with the word "apart" (fallen).</note>

At this point, however, it is necessary to describe the distinction between the **Lower and Upper Rocks**, which are partly a hindrance and partly a benefit to the mine. Though it is their nature to increase within the earth, no stone serves the subsequent work at all, for they contain no **nourishment** <note>original: *nutrimentum*</note> within themselves; thus they must also perish. ## Concerning the Distress of Water.

There is now something that displeases me greatly regarding the workings of **fissures** <term>Klüffte</term> and **veins** <term>Gänge</term>: the **Distress of Water** <term>Wasser-Noht</term>. For it is undeniably obvious that the fissures and veins of the earth carry water—both **surface water** <note>original: *Tag-Wasser*</note> and **ground water**. If one opens them up, one makes them active and strengthens them, often leading to the ruin of good **mines** <term>Berg-wercke</term>. # The First Book, Chapter 34.

People, although they do not know where **fluxes** <note>original: *Flüsse*; likely referring to fluorite or similar glass-like minerals that assist in melting</note> come from, can make nothing of them. They are indeed fluid when they are put into the fire, but one can introduce nothing into them, for they allow no air into themselves, nor any of the qualities in the air that might make them more noble. For it is a strange thing in nature: when something good is driven out of a **body** <note>original Latin: *corpore*</note>, especially by force, it will not go back in. For when life is taken from a person, it cannot be given back to him; the **body** <note>German: *Cörper*</note> accepts it no more, even if he died naturally—though for God, it is indeed possible. 

But I am not writing here of miracles, but of what is natural and based on experience; I rightly leave the other matters aside. And it is very strange that the **body** <note>original Latin: *corpus*</note> of deceased metals is so beautiful, whereas other **bodies** <note>original Latin: *corpora*</note> decay and come to nothing—though eventually, over a long time, that happens to the metal as well. But in death, it is as beautiful as any glass and still retains some color, especially if it was **marcasitic** <term>marcasitisch</term> <note>pertaining to marcasite, a mineral similar to pyrite but with a different crystal structure</note>. 

From this, the colors of the marcasites can be recognized; for one finds fine green, blue, white, and brown fluxes, just as the **flowers of metals** <note>original Latin: *flores Metallorum*; a term for the refined essences or sublimates of minerals</note> once were, which were then drawn out of three **bodies** <note>original Latin: *corporibus*</note>. They might be mistaken for precious stones, but they are too soft and waste away up here [on the surface], as is the nature of all **deep-stone** <term>Unterstein</term> <note>minerals or rocks formed deep underground</note> when they reach the **upper air** <note>original: *Oberlufft*</note>. ## Of Stone-Meal.

It is also to be observed here above in this our air that no vapor or wind rises up in vain; it resolves itself again into another work; hence come so many meteors <note>original: *meteora*; in this era, the term referred to all atmospheric phenomena including wind, rain, and vapors, not just falling stars</note>; the inner earth has just such meteors as well. For the vapor that rises from the fiery exhalations <term>Feurwitterung</term> <note>the subterranean "weather" or vapors produced by the earth's internal heat</note> of the ores or metals produces this stone-meal. Wherever it then falls, it crumbles more and becomes very abundant, yielding a harmful sediment. When it moves to the places where ores are located, especially where they are rising up <note>growing or forming</note>, it hinders their color. One sees this in the Mansfeld shale <note>a famous copper-bearing slate deposit in Germany</note>, where it has settled between the layers of the ore so that it cannot easily be removed; for it robs much, and consumes the shimmer and glimmer. It pursues these <note>the shiny metallic qualities</note> as long as it is in the work, and one can hardly be entirely rid of it. Because of this, one loses much of that ore or metal; for according to the nature of its fire, when it joins with them, it makes them volatile <note>original: *volatile*; substances that evaporate or turn to gas when heated</note> again, and it sticks fast, burns hard, and carries the metal away with it, especially that which is partially melted. # Book 1, Chapter 35

...the stone is that very same meal. Thus, the marrow <note>original: *Marck*; referring to a soft, fatty, or pithy mineral substance found inside rocks</note> is the softest part of all and clings very readily to the quartz <term>Kißling</term> <note>a historical term for pebbles, quartz, or flinty river stones</note>, for it originates from them. For when a fire or vapor reaches a quartz stone and burns it, the exterior—the shell—becomes such meal. The water, however, enters inside—especially if it was somewhat hollow within—and draws the interior into itself to become marrow. This is especially caused by the extreme cold fire; for heat and cold must perform their work down below, where they are not as tempered as they are up here on the surface. Wherever they strike and cast their rays, such meal and marrow are formed by that same heat and subterranean cold.

Just as the sun, where it shines and casts its rays, performs its own work—which I call the upper burns <term>Uredines</term> <note>original: *Uredines*; a Latin term for blights or scorching winds. The author is comparing solar radiation to subterranean mineral "rays"</note>. These rays, however, have their subterranean source in the metals—the cold rays from cold metals, the hot rays from hot ones. If they should strike someone, let him beware! Just as they cause damage to the young fruits of the earth, they also harm the stones, waters, and air. 

If someone should fall into such misfortune beneath the earth and receive a "blast" <note>original: *Schuß*; likely referring to a sudden discharge of gas or a rock burst caused by internal pressure</note>, let him accept it as best he can and see how he may be rid of its effects; it is better that he stay out of the way and let the stone "shoot" so that it may turn to meal and marrow. 

Such meal, however, clogs the pores <note>original: *Poros*; the tiny openings or passages within the rock strata</note> and creates a stagnation of air <term>Wettersatz</term> <note>a traditional mining term for foul, stagnant, or unbreathable air that fails to circulate</note> so that the fresh air cannot follow after. For even the fire cannot lift it, and it thereafter consumes the stone continuously. Thus, the stone-marrow works from the inside out until they finally come together and form such a strange potter’s meal <note>original: *Töpener Mehl*; likely a reference to a fine, clay-like mineral dust used in ceramics</note>. They rasp into themselves the subterranean quartz stones, both coarse and small, which finally consume themselves within it and

## On the Self-Blower.

The "Self-Blower" is an instrument that corrects the "foul weather" <note>original: *böses Wetter*; a mining term for dangerous or stagnant gases in a mine shaft</note> or the displaced air. For displaced air does not create stone—otherwise everything containing it would turn to stone—rather, stone forms where the internal fire draws in [substance] instead of air and dries it, though without igniting it. This is clearly seen when one strikes off a fragment <note>original: *Haucke*; a chip or flake of rock</note> with a pick; one sees how it leaps out. This leaping fragment allows us to understand how Nature creates stone, and likewise how it creates ore or metal, for they are essentially the same thing. Only noble gemstones have a different origin, arising from "sweet waters" <note>fresh water, as opposed to mineralized or salt water</note>.

Now, in such an instrument, fire and air are brought together; it draws its power and material from the "foul weather." The fire consumes whatever "heavy" elements are within that air and lightens <note>original: *erleuchtet*; likely meaning to make less dense or to purify the air</note> the remaining part which it carries. This blower is constructed as a sphere made of copper, about the size of a head. And I say this with good reason: where the roasting fire always ruled with a constant strength, no metal would remain in the entire ore; but that it shines a little is more the fault of the uneven fire than that it should be of service to the metal, not to mention the cruel stench it brings forth from the **waste products** <note>original: *excrementis*</note>, as well as from the ruined, sour **minerals** <note>original: *Mineralibus*</note> and dried-up juices, which it attacks with smoke; this then brings up the **mine-sicknesses** <term>mine-sicknesses: respiratory illnesses, such as silicosis or poisoning, caused by inhaling toxic fumes or dust in mining and smelting</term>, which one would otherwise have to fetch down in the shafts, so that not only the workers in the mines but also the smelters before the fire receive their portion of the fire. For although it is not directed at the metal, but at the rock types and wild stones that are alongside and with it, it is nonetheless a great lack of understanding that one cannot even slightly see from such an unclean ore—which is then brought in—how the ore first grows, and how it only lies there moistened, and how very hard it sticks to the same before nature brings it forth without harm and without a roasting fire; for if nature were to roast in this way under the earth, we would not have much metal, but rather much coal and limestone, as indeed the best part flies away here above <note>The author suggests that the "best part" of the metal is volatile and escapes as vapor during the roasting process.</note>.

# CHAPTER XLV.
## OF THE GLOWING FIRE,
->or<-
### Of the Roasting Fire.

<image-desc>Faint ink sketch in the left margin next to the chapter heading, resembling a long, narrow triangular object or a stylus.</image-desc>

This fire is directed at the **metallic bodies** <note>original: *corpora metallorum*</note>, which it consumes through the materials they naturally possess that are prone to it. For this reason, I must hold this fire in high regard; the bodies that remain become quite malleable, while the **waste products** <note>original: *exuvia*, literally "cast-off skins," referring here to the impurities or dross separated from the metal</note> are left behind on the spot. The very best thing about them is that through the glowing heat, they cast off everything that ought to be removed, while the other part remains.

It would be even better, however, if one first placed the material into a **washing works** <term>washing works: a facility (Waschwerk) where ore was crushed and washed with water to separate heavy metallic particles from lighter waste rock before the smelting process began</term>, so that the water might remove whatever it can with less damage before one hurries to the fire with it. For be that as it may, once the fire is applied, it attacks. I cannot find fault with the roasting process, but when something is lost during the roasting that should have remained, that is too much and it "robs" the metal. The scent reveals this: if a roasting smells more like raw minerals than like metal, then the metal is already partially destroyed.

For look at **iron**: it gives off its **dross** <note>original: *Exuvium*</note>, and **copper** also yields its **sinter** <term>sinter: the scale or oxidation crust that forms on the surface of heated metal</term> or **slag**. However, if it flares up violently, it robs and consumes the iron. For this reason, **pit-coal** <note>original: *SteinKohlen*</note>—which contains so much **sulfur**—is not good for iron; it burns the iron and carries it away so that nothing but idle sinter remains, which is a pity. I hold it as most certain that one should not [use] one of these things alone...

Of the Glowing Fire.

...not only to the metals from which one wishes to extract good results, but one should also not apply it to herbs, roots, stones, and the like, or subject them to the "evil fire" <note>An "evil fire" likely refers to a fire that is too intense or uncontrolled, which destroys the "life" or essence of the material instead of purifying it</note>. Therefore, I also praise the roasting <note>original: *Glüen*</note> here, where—as is done in **Mansfeld** <note>a major historical copper-mining district in Germany</note>—one piles up a heap of ore and sets it alight, letting it then glow through on its own to burn away what needs to be removed.

The metal in **Sweden** does this too, by the heat of the sun in summer; it then flows nicely together and purifies itself so beautifully that it eventually becomes superfine. I hold these methods in high regard. However, with the exception of these two metals—**copper** and **iron**—it is not advisable to roast the others in the open. Even though **gold** and **silver** can also be roasted, it is not particularly beneficial.

All the others do not roast well; therefore, they must go where they are with the others and be processed together with them—the same applies to **minerals** <note>original: *Mineralia*</note> and the weak metals. There is, however, a twofold "glowing fire" and two kinds of roasting necessary for the metal. One kind of roasting is this: as in Mansfeld, where one sets the heaps of **shale** <term>shale: specifically *Kupferschiefer* or copper shale, the ore-bearing rock typical of the Mansfeld region</term> on fire with a wisp of straw and lets them smolder within themselves and glow like a heap of coals until the ore is heated through. This roasting should take place in iron or copper vessels which do not melt when metal is inside them, nor do they leak what is contained within. This is not known to everyone; for just as you can boil water in a tin or lead pot or pan without the pot melting, so too can you roast a metal in iron or copper vessels—especially copper—without the vessel melting away.

### Chapter 45 of the First Book

The second kind of **roasting** involves a great loss of metals and the expense of the vessels, especially if you roast in a **robbing-furnace** <note>original: *Räuber*; a type of furnace or crucible known for "stealing" or absorbing the metal being processed</note>, or in glass or other clay vessels. Although these may be reinforced with iron or copper plates, when the great heat arrives, they become prone to melting and are thus not suitable for the metal. Clay, glass, and slag are not metals; therefore, the metal suffers a decrease within them and cannot be properly mastered. For this reason, look closely at what kind of metal you wish to treat, so that you may provide it with the rightful fire. This is indeed the very best fire for metals and for their **transmutation** <note>the alchemical process of changing one substance into another, such as lead into gold</note>. For you can see it even in the hardest metals, which cast off their **bodies** <note>original: *corpora*</note> during the roasting. For tell me, what is the **body** of iron or copper other than its slag? Its **soul** <note>original: *Anima*</note> or its **tincture** <note>the concentrated spiritual essence or coloring principle of a metal</note> departs, as you can clearly see in the smelting; when you throw them into the glowing heat, they fly away in a flame. Therefore, one must have them "doubled" <note>likely referring to the reinforcement or capture of these volatile spirits</note> so that they serve the metal and allow it to be worked correctly.

Otherwise, roasting is also useful for the **bodies of stones**, as it turns them into **lime** <note>original: *calce*</note>. But those who have until now made the **metallic calces** <note>original: *calces Metallorum*; the powdery remains (oxides) left after a metal has been burned</note> in a simple heat have only obtained the **calces of the cast-off bodies** <note>original: *Exuviorum corporum calces*; the "husks" or empty shells of the metal after the spirit has fled</note>. Therefore, neither they nor anyone else should wonder why they have accomplished or achieved nothing good. For let everyone think rightly for themselves what the **calcination** <note>the process of heating a substance to high temperatures to change its physical or chemical state</note> in a **reverberatory furnace** <note>original: *reverber*; an open-fire furnace where the flame is "thrown back" onto the material</note>—that same harsh roasting—is supposed to do or preserve when the vessels (even the earthen ones) are not **sealed with lute** <note>original: *verlutiret*; sealed with a specialized alchemical clay or cement to make them airtight</note>, and the **Mercury** <note>original: *Mercurius*; here referring to the volatile "spirit" or quicksilver essence of the metal</note>...

This fire must be categorized among the cold fires, for they consume. This consumption occurs within the cold fire, for it possesses the same nature as burning fire—it shines and burns. Instead, it is good where it warms—that is, where something lies in between, such as water, so that I may enjoy the heat of the fire and the water together: warmth. 

In the same way, warmth occurs when I have the metal in a vessel, so that only the heat of that same vessel communicates the warmth to the metal. Now, the warmth of glass or clay does this well, but it is harmful; for it is not full, but empty of such a substance that should be serviceable to the metal and also strengthen it—not the harsh heat, but the gentle warmth. 

Therefore one sees, as I have often said regarding the vessels of the alchemists, that they do not truly consider the **matter** <note>original: *materia*; here meaning the physical material the vessel is made of</note> of the equipment, but only the forms—how many **beaks and bellies** <note>refers to the various spouts (*Schnäbel*) and rounded glass bodies (*Bäuche*) of alchemical stills like alembics and retorts</note> they should have. In between these, it must be so distressed <note>original: *geängstiget*; a term for applying pressure or intense heat to force a transformation</note> that not much of it remains; for that is what heat does when it gains the upper hand.

[informed by] a magnet of the compass where **East**, **West**, **South**, or **North** <note>original: *Morgen, Abend, Mittag, oder Mitternacht*—early German mining terminology often used times of day to indicate the four cardinal directions</note> may be; as well as truly to fathom this or that rock in its **strikes** <term>strike: the horizontal direction or compass bearing of a geological feature, such as an ore vein</term>, also to have and hold them together with their emergence, for good instruction, regarding both the long and short mountain ranges, how they extend at the top for the longest time in a uniform shape. The forms of such mountain ranges are varied: Firstly, one part contains many glistening, talc-bearing shales, such as **silver- and lead-mountains**; another part is in a coarse rock, in which there is little shale and talc—these are to be recognized by their hardness; another part are rocks in which copper and **tin-flowers** <note>original: *Zwitter-Blumen*; "Zwitter" was a common term for tin-ore among miners, and "flowers" refers to the crystalline or bloom-like appearance of the mineral</note> shine forth; and in part also flat **seams** <term>seam (Flöz): a layer or bed of ore-bearing rock</term> and shale-rock, in which copper ore is also formed. Therefore, it is well to be gathered from Nature that because of various forms, various **fruits** <note>the "fruits" of the earth refer to the ores and minerals produced by natural processes</note> are also attained; there, one finds in the **Southern mountains**, which are better than those parts toward the **West**, which are called the **secondary mountains** or ends, between which a center of perfection is always ordered.

## CHAPTER IV.

# Of Silver Ore, its Rock Formation, Action, Nature, and Striking Veins.

<margin>A</margin>Silver ore is also formed in its own stone, arising from a quite perfect nature and a beautiful, noble earth, and from the most stable, clear **sulfur**, its **salt**, and **mercury** <note>original symbols: Sulphur, Salt, and ☿. These are the "Tria Prima" or three primary substances of alchemy believed to constitute all matter</note>, which join together in a mixture with a powerful bond. This occurs in such a way that it appears to be of a lower degree than **gold** <note>original symbol: ☉, the Sun</note>, and yet, after gold, it is the very best and most stable metal among all those that follow. It suffers very little loss when exposed to fire <note>original: *Verbrennligkeit*; referring to the fact that silver, like gold, does not oxidize or "burn away" easily during smelting</note> and can be brought out of the fire and separated by itself or from other **metals**. That which its naturally well-disposed stone—the natural silver **rock formation** <term>Gebürge; in early mining, this referred both to the mountain and the specific geological host rock</term>—causes, nevertheless follows the heavenly influence and the night-light of the **Moon** <note>original symbol: ☽</note>. For this reason, the most **silver veins** are found in the northern <note>original: *mitnächtigen*; literally "midnight," a traditional term for the North</note> lands. For just as the Moon has the Sun to its right and receives its light from it, so and in like manner the silver veins and silver stone have the gold veins to their right. <margin>A</margin>Thus, a "root" is compared to the noble **Lunar Queen** <note>original: *Lunariæ*; the feminine personification of silver in alchemy</note>, from which the **gold vein** receives all the more strength and power in its mixture; the mountains themselves attain these qualities from their roots. ### Chapter 5 of the 2nd Book.

<margin>A</margin>
Copper ore in veins is often rich in gold and silver, depending on whether it is surrounded by a good host-rock <term>Zech-Gestein; a specific type of Permian sedimentary rock common in German mining regions</term> and set with worthy stones, provided that no other metals or minerals are nearby that corrode or consume it. Likewise, copper ore is also found in shale-work, mixed with many "leafy" mountains <note>original: *Lauben-Gebür*; likely referring to foliated or thin-layered rock structures that resemble leaves</note>, from which such ♀ <note>The symbol for the planet Venus, used by alchemists and miners to represent copper.</note>—copper, I mean—is only extracted with difficulty through poor smelting. It also yields much iron and immature copper speiss, which "robs" the copper during roasting <note>Roasting involves heating the ore in air to remove volatile elements like sulfur and arsenic; if done poorly, the copper can be lost in the process.</note> and makes it brittle. However, the most profitable copper ores are found in the Orient, in Hungary, in Bohemia, and Silesia, as well as Thuringia, Hesse, and Vogtland. This type is found around Trutnov <note>original: *Trautenau*; a city in the modern-day Czech Republic known for its mining history</note>, where it breaks in seams everywhere, with a sandy ore in the footwall <term>Liegenden; the layer of rock underlying a mineral seam or vein</term>. Where it breaks heavily in shale-work or tuff-stone, they call it "cleaved shale" [fissile shale]; these are poor in silver and must otherwise all be roasted.

In some places, it breaks quite purely in blue-shale and brown, or reddish, copper-glance with a mountain-green <note>original: *Berggrün*; malachite, a green copper carbonate mineral</note>. ### CHAPTER VII.

## Nature, and Striking 
## Veins.

Lead ore is formed through the heavenly influence of the black and cold <term>Saturn <note>The manuscript uses the symbol ♄ for Saturn, the planet traditionally associated with lead in alchemy due to its heavy, "cold" nature.</note></term>, out of uncooked, watery sulfur, impure <term>mercury <note>The manuscript uses the symbol ☿ for mercury, representing the principle of fluidity and metallic essence.</note></term>, and salt. # Concerning Lead Ore

The true <term>lead glance <note>original: Bleygläntze; galena, the primary mineral form of lead sulfide.</note></term> and ores, however, yield a half or a third part lead, being little mixed with other metals. If the luster of one of the other metals is found within it—possessing the upper hand and preference—then these are not true, simple <term>lead veins <note>original: Bley-Gäng; the paths or lodes within the rock where the ore is found.</note></term>. Instead, the lead has matched and united itself with gold, such that they are mixed stones; for the rocks of the <term>lead-bearing mountains <note>original: Bley-Gebürg; the specific geological formations or mountain ranges containing lead deposits.</note></term> are far more wondrous, with unique accidental variations.

This happens, therefore, not without cause; for according to his heavy weight, he provides the lightest <term>remedies <note>original: remedia; medicinal preparations.</note></term> for all melancholic blood and things. # On Lead Ore
CA.

...[of God] the mountains of metals; if only mankind used them correctly, then everything would be without lack, and a good supply would be at hand; but where one uses such things ignorantly, one has little profit from them. For just as a chain is made from its <term>soul <note>original: Seele; in early modern mining and alchemy, this refers to the essential spiritual or chemical principle that gives a metal its properties.</note></term>, which draws and joins together the joints and gold-fissures, as well as silver, so it also possesses a particular spirit that can be distilled into a water through the visible and invisible <term>alembic <note>original: Helm; literally the "helmet" or cap of a distillation apparatus; here used metaphorically to describe how vapors in the earth condense into minerals.</note></term>. Just as nature in the earth turns such waters into ice upon its veins, hardening them into a signpost and certain mark by which everyone recognizes that it is a <term>lead-streak <note>original: Bleyschweiff; literally "lead-tail," referring to a fine-grained, shimmering variety of galena that often appears as a thin streak, indicating a larger vein is nearby.</note></term> and a sure indication of its own lead vein—whether it has other metallic deposits or not, it is all the more pleasant and better for it.

The best lead veins, however, and the most consistent among all of them, are the water-blue, scaly, talc-like <term>shale rocks</term>, gritty and with elongated <term>fluor-quartz <note>original: Fluß-Quark; a historical term combining "Fluß" (fluorite) and "Quark" (an old mining term for quartz or base rock).</note></term>, or sprinkled in circles and not twisted, but rather coarsely fissured, with horizontal veins and uniform structures, in some parts not unlike the silver mountains. Some lead mountains are also made of a white-scaly talc-shale full of "wild" <term>garnets</term>, or undulating here and there, in which silver-rich lead ores show themselves.

## CHAPTER VIII.

# On Tin / its Mountains / Workings / Mists / Stocks / Seams / Drops and Striking Veins.

Tin ore is formed within a sandstone, in accordance with the celestial influence of **Jupiter** <note>original: Jovis; in alchemy and early natural philosophy, tin was the metal cosmologically linked to the planet Jupiter.</note>. It appears dark-black and brown, purple-colored, greyish, or black-shining, and is composed of a mercury, salt, and a small amount of mixed sulfur. With these are mingled unpleasant, coarse, sulfurous **vapors** <note>original: Bradem; an archaic term for the exhalations or fumes within the earth believed to condense into minerals.</note> which embody and bind together to create the metal tin. It is because of these unpleasant vapors that every kind of tin becomes "crunchy" <note>This refers to the "cry of tin," a characteristic crackling sound made when bending a bar of the metal.</note> and brittle, so much so that it also makes all other metals melted with it unpleasant and brittle.

Such tin, or **tin-ore** <term>Zwitter <note>original: Zwitter; a specific historical term in Saxon mining for tin-bearing rock or cassiterite, often found in granitic formations.</note></term>, occurs in three types and colors: namely, in veins, in mists, or in "stocks" <note>Massive, irregular ore bodies as opposed to thin veins.</note>. It also contains three kinds of **impurities** <term>Wildnuß <note>original: Wildnuß; literally "wildness," referring to the non-valuable minerals or gangue rock that grow alongside the ore.</note></term>, such as **crusts** <note>original: Schöll; likely referring to rocky shells or shaly inclusions.</note>, **pyrite** <note>original: Kiß; historical spelling of Kies, usually referring to iron pyrites.</note>, and **iron-stain** <note>original: Eisenmahl; iron-bearing minerals that color the ore.</note>, from which it yields "hard work" <note>Refers to ore that is difficult to smelt or process due to these contaminants.</note>. Its colors are primarily black, slate-brown, and yellow.

Such sandstone and tin-ore mountains contain many mighty, powerful, upright veins and faces within them which reveal themselves at the surface <note>original: am Tag; literally "at the day," a mining term for the surface or outcropping.</note> with tin-ore. Some have very rich "milling-work" <note>Ore suitable for being crushed in a stamp mill.</note>; the pyrite in some must be roasted; and some contains much talc and **mica** <term>KatzenSilber <note>original: KatzenSilber; literally "cat's silver," a mocking name for mica because its metallic shine deceptively resembles silver.</note></term>, which is the "nourishment" of the tin-ore, in which it likes to reside. Other types appear glimmering and iron-stained, and some also strike through **flint-stone** <note>original: Feurgestein; likely referring to quartz or other hard silicate rocks that strike sparks.</note>,

### CHAPTER IX.
# Of Mercury Ore and its Veins.

Mercury ore is produced within its own mountain stones according to its nature, consisting of salt-earths and nimble, volatile earths—of a moist, greasy, slimy, watery oiliness <note>original: Olität; an alchemical term referring to the "oily" or flammable principle thought to exist within minerals.</note>. This is mixed with the most subtle, raw-sulfurous, cooked earth in the weakest, most gradual connection, acting as a premature, pleasant fruit of all particular metals.

<margin>Mercury</margin>
Mercury demonstrates its virtue in many strange ways and shares its active nature and power with minerals and metallic sulfurs, as well as bordering upon **antimonial stones** <term>Spießgläsige Gestein <note>Stibnite or antimony ore, which often resembles glass when processed.</note></term>. It is also readily found where the **tin-mountains** lie higher than the **silver veins**. This requires a much-repeated, powerful action upon other ores, manifesting also in other foreign stones; it is pushed and drawn through the juices <note>original: Safft; the "liquors" or liquid precursors believed to form minerals in the earth.</note> of minerals and metals that are befriended to one another. These produce many strange, miraculous births, making it agreeable to the metals, so that goldsmiths are able to **amalgamate** and gild with it.

It is also made into metallic pigments, prepared into oil and water for health, and **sublimated** <note>The process of vaporizing and re-solidifying a substance to purify it.</note> to become the most terrible poison for etching. It is a true **thief** <note>original: Räuber (robber); refers to mercury’s ability to "steal" or dissolve other metals like gold and silver into itself.</note>, for it gladly takes away and carries with it whatever effort and expense one has spent upon it...

# On the Nature of Gold, etc.

My best and most beautiful color shines and reveals itself according to the <term>vitriolic natures</term> <note>Original: "Vitriolitäten." This refers to sulfate minerals (vitriols), which were essential in alchemical experiments for producing acids and "spirits."</note> and translucent juices, which, according to my nature, penetrate their mountains at the appropriate time; from this they are extracted in a joyful and more lovely, pleasing form, etched away, [appearing] green as sealing wax, green as goose droppings <note>Original: "Ganß-Koht." A common historical descriptor for specific shades of dull, yellowish-green minerals, often associated with weathered ores.</note>, green-coated, blue as a beautiful sapphire, and so on; also at times shimmering like <term>water-pyrite</term> <note>Original: "Wasser-Kiß," likely referring to marcasite or iridescent iron pyrites found in damp mining environments.</note>, among all of which my red color with the white is the best and most heartily to be desired. I ignite myself gladly in vitriol and promote it, after the descent of its underlying green substance, to the deep red <term>Spirit</term> <note>Original: "Spiritu." In alchemy, a "spirit" is a volatile substance or essence released through distillation.</note>, out of which, after its laxative cleansing <note>A metaphor for the purification process, "purging" the substance of its dross or impurities.</note>, comes the right and desired <term>water of Saturn</term> <note>Original: "aqua Saturni." In this context, it refers to a "philosophical" solvent or a specific stage of the alchemical work, rather than simple lead-water.</note>, the true Acid Spring. From this I myself, as well as other metals, <term>animals and vegetables</term> <note>Original: "animalia & vegetabilia," representing the three kingdoms of nature: mineral, animal, and vegetable.</note>, have my origin and life; for out of it, and it alone, do all metals and minerals arise and spring; they have their beginning and origin from the same, for it is that same life-giving water of which no common miner knows, but is known only to the <term>Philosophers</term> <note>Original: "Philosophis," meaning alchemists or those who study the hidden laws of nature.</note>. It works the minerals and metals of various kinds, such as stalactitic, crystalline, pure, white, and native—just as refined sugar is found in a blue slate-work. # Of the Universal of this entire World. #

But because I hope that those who are intent on turning toward <term>Wisdom</term> <note>original: "Weißheit"; often referring to *Sophia* or divine insight in alchemical and mystical traditions.</note> with a truly faithful heart will pay closer attention than the base and mad world—to which these writings of mine will give no small cause and help, in that everything has indeed been made as clear as was ever possible, just as the kindled <term>Light</term> <note>A common metaphor for spiritual and intellectual illumination in Hermetic texts.</note> shall be further purified, so that the beginning learner may have a completely full radiance before his eyes without any darkening, from the beginning until the grave: I have therefore taken such pains upon myself to discover that which all the world has kept secret, and hidden until its very end, and preserved with silence until their graves.

But that I have done such a thing, I have not done to attain honor and glory thereby, but rather so that God's gracious <term>Providence</term> <note>original: "Vorsehung"</note> should not be falsified, but should remain open and before the eyes of certain descendants—even the very fewest—so that they may appear helpful to their poor, needy fellow-Christians, and make them partakers of the grace and mercy of God the Father. Although my soul is troubled from the heart when I think of what I have done, and how I write so freely and uncovered into the open field, and do not know who will be the possessor of this book after my death: Yet I will hope, whoever he may be, that he will let my preceding warning in my previous and current writings be commended to him day and night, so that he may handle and use this book in such a way,

...that he must answer for it before the **Divine Majesty**.

And as concerns the **Vitriol** <term>Vitriol</term> <note>Historically, vitriol referred to various sulfate minerals—such as iron or copper sulfate—that were essential in early chemistry for producing "spirit of vitriol" (sulfuric acid) and served as a foundational material for alchemical transmutation.</note> further, I should rightly mention it in my practical instructions where I shall treat and write of **minerals** in general; Yet because this is such a noble **mineral**, to which none in all of Nature can be compared, and because **Vitriol** is more befriended and more closely related to **Metals** than all others—as a **Vitriol** or **Crystalline** <note>original: "Cristallin"; referring to the crystallized salts obtained from metals dissolved in acid.</note> can be made from all **Metals** (for **Crystal** and **Vitriol** are recognized as one and the same)—I have therefore not wished to deprive it of its praise, nor to postpone it until later: but rather, as is fitting, I have preferred it over the other **Minerals** and granted it the first place after the **Metals**: for (excluding all other **Metals** and **Minerals**) this alone is sufficient to make the highly blessed **Stone** <term>Philosopher's Stone</term> <note>The "Great Work" or *Lapis Philosophorum*, the legendary substance capable of perfecting base matter into gold and providing a universal medicine.</note> from it, which nothing else in the world can imitate; although in particular cases some other substances may help to promote the work, just as **Antimony** <term>Antimony</term> <note>A brittle, silvery-white metalloid used in purifying gold; alchemists often personified it as the "Grey Wolf."</note> alone is **Master** enough, as shall be mentioned in its proper place. # Manual Procedure

Once the ruby-colored golden water is ready, distill it over so that it is combined; in this way it becomes one, just as it was originally. # On the Sulfur of Gold <note>original: "Sulphure Solis." In alchemy, "Sulfur" refers to the combustible, active, or "soul" principle of a metal.</note>

...part **flowers of sulfur** <note>original: "florum sulphuris." A fine powder produced by sublimating natural sulfur.</note>, and let it smoke away again under the **muffle** <note>A clay oven or enclosure used to protect the material from direct flame while allowing high heat.</note>. The powder that remains should be heated to a glow with a stronger fire; then, pour it into the **spirit of wine** <note>original: "spiritum vini." High-proof distilled alcohol.</note>. Perform this labor six times, until finally the gold powder becomes as soft and spongy as hard butter. Dry it gently, for it flows very easily. 

Then, take a coated flask which has a hollow tube or **vent** <note>original: "spiraculum." A breathing hole or small opening in the vessel.</note> at the back; **seal** <note>original: "lutire." To seal the joints of laboratory glassware using a specialized paste or clay called "lute."</note> a helm <note>The top part of a still.</note> onto it and attach a **receiver** <note>original: "recipienten." The vessel that collects the distilled liquid.</note>. Place it empty into a strong **sand bath** <note>original: "Sand-Capellen." A container of sand used to distribute heat evenly to a glass vessel.</note> and give it gentle heat at first, then stronger heat, until the flask in the sand is nearly glowing. Then, take the softened yet well-dried gold powder (otherwise the glass will shatter), warm it slightly, and pour it into the tube at the back. Stop the opening quickly, and nimble red drops will soon enter the helm. Maintain the fire at this degree until nothing more rises and no more drops fall into the **receiver**. 

Note, however, that in the **receiver**, there should be placed **spirit of wine** of the highest and best quality, weighing three times as much as the **gold calx** <note>original: "Gold-Kalck." A metal reduced to a powder through calcination (heating).</note>, into which the drops of gold shall fall.

Then take this **spirit of wine**, into which the golden drops have fallen, and put it into a **Pelican** <note>original: "Pelican." A specialized circulatory vessel with two "arms" that return the condensed vapors to the base, resembling the myth of the pelican feeding its young with its own blood.</note>. **Seal it hermetically** <note>original: "sigillirs hermeticè." To create an airtight seal by melting the glass neck of the vessel shut.</note> and **circulate** <note>original: "circuliers." The process of repeatedly evaporating and condensing a liquid within a closed vessel.</note> it for one month. From this, a blood-red stone will form, which flows in the fire like wax. Crush it small and rub **silver calx** into it. Melt them together in a strong crucible. When it has cooled, pour it into **strong water** <note>original: "aqua fort." Usually *aqua fortis* or nitric acid, used here to dissolve the silver and leave the gold.</note>, and a black powder will fall to the bottom. Melt this powder, and you will find as much good gold as the gold powder and the spirit of wine, together with half—

## On the Particular Operation of Saturn, including the Extraction of its Soul and Salt.

The greater part of the world considers **Saturn** <note>original: "Saturnum." The alchemical name for the metal Lead.</note> or **Lead** to be a lowly and worthless metal, and it is often used for very minor and trivial things; yet, if one truly recognized its inner nature, much more useful and excellent things could be prepared from it. Since I have then intended and resolved, in this my final report and practical manual, to clarify all my previous writings <margin><unclear>To 1</unclear></margin> and to leave them behind as a memorable testament, so that even the simple man, though endowed with little understanding, may recognize what I have written before—and of which I myself shall be a witness after the resurrection of my flesh: that I have told no untruth, but have perhaps done more than was proper, and have explained here and there in my writings all that which others before me kept secret—I have therefore also resolved to explain and report from a true and solid foundation all the **Particulars** <term>Particularia: specific alchemical procedures intended to achieve a particular transmutation or medicinal result, as opposed to the "Universal" work of the Philosopher's Stone.</term> which I have previously mentioned many times in words and outlined in a philosophical manner. I do this in such a way that, in my final years, I wish once again to admonish the one who receives this, my last explanation, by his conscience (as I have before), to pay heed and to observe with diligent <margin>A</margin> care that he [treat] this revelation—which is sent to him in no other way than through the will, counsel, and providence of the Creator of all creatures—in a special manner; the true- <note>original: "das wah-". This is a catchword for "das wahre" (the true) which would begin the following page.</note>

<summary>The author introduces a new section on the alchemical secrets of lead (Saturn), describing it as a misunderstood metal of great potential. Practical Operation

## The short way to make the Sulfur and the Salt of Antimony is as follows.

<margin>Water?</margin>
Take one pound each of good vitriol, common salt, and unslaked lime, and eight **lots** <term>original: "Loht"; a historical German unit of weight, approximately 14-17 grams or half an ounce</term> of sal ammoniac. Crush everything small and put it into a glass flask. Pour three pounds of common wine vinegar over it and let it stand sealed in the warmth for one day. Then put everything together into a **retort** <note>a glass vessel with a long, downward-pointing neck used for distilling liquids</note>, attach a receiver, and drive it out as one is accustomed to driving out **aqua fortis** <term>literally "strong water"; usually nitric acid, here used as a potent solvent</term>. Take one pound of this distilled liquid <note>original: "liquoris"</note> and one pound of common salt <note>original: "salis communis"</note> and **rectify** <note>to purify a liquid by repeated distillation</note> it once more very slowly, so that nothing cloudy passes over, but everything becomes beautifully clear. Then take one pound of finely powdered **glass of antimony** <term>original: "vitrum antimonii"; a reddish, translucent glass made from roasted antimony ore</term>, pour the spirits over it, **lute** it well <note>seal the vessel's joints with an airtight paste</note>, and digest it until everything is dissolved. Then gently draw off the water in a **Bain-Marie** <term>original: "B. M." or "Balneum Mariae"; a water bath used for gentle, even heating</term>, and a black, thick-fluid matter remains at the bottom, somewhat dry. Lay this upon a glass plate and set it in the cellar.
<margin>X</margin>
In this way, a red oil flows from it, leaving a few dregs <note>original: "feces"</note> behind. Coagulate this red oil very gently on the ashes until it has become dry; then pour the best **spirit of wine** <term>original: "spiritum vini"; concentrated alcohol</term> over it, and the spirit of wine will extract the tincture as blood-red. Pour off the colored liquid and pour more spirit of wine onto the residue until no more redness appears. In this way, you have the **Tincture** or **Sulfur of Antimony**. It works wonders in medicine and (as was also said before in the first process) is not much inferior to **potable gold** <term>original: "auro potabili"; a legendary alchemical medicine thought to grant long life</term>.

# End of the Procedures of Brother Basilius Valentinus regarding the Philosopher's Stone <note>original: Lapidem Philosophorum</note>.

This Universal Work consists of four chapters or operations: The first part of the preparation is the preparation <note>original: præparatio</note> of Gold <note>symbol: ☉</note> with its corresponding solar water; the end of the first part is the purple-colored Gold powder, where the Gold has been well-purged and prepared for further use.

The second part of the preparatory work is the preparation of the Mercury, Sulphur, and Salt of the Philosophers <note>original: ☿, Sulphuris & Salis Philosophorum</note> derived from Antimony <note>symbol: ♁</note> and Iron <note>symbol: ♂</note> until the golden water is thickened; this is the end of the second operation, and herewith the "double mercury" is made.

The third part of the preparatory work is the preparation of the Sulphur of Gold <note>original: Sulphuris Solis</note>, from which the true <term>potable gold</term> <note>original: aurum potabile; a legendary liquid medicine thought to be a universal cure-all made from dissolved gold</note> is to be made; with this, the third operation—and thus the most difficult labor in the Work—is completed.

The fourth part is now the last and final work, acting as the last conjunction and joining together of all things into one, where such things are perfected and carried through to the end.

->Following is the Distillation of the Spirit of Wine.<- <note>original: Sequitur Distillatio Spiritus Vini</note>

# Revelation of the hidden techniques.

## Now follows the preparation of the fiery Spirit of Wine.

One should have an instrument made of copper <note>symbol: ♀; associated with the planet Venus</note> / <unclear>d</unclear> in the middle / and the parts below and above the holes <unclear>k</unclear> should be removable / as well as above the half-flask <note>original: Kolben; a glass vessel used in distillation</note>. Upon this, place an alembic <note>original: alembicum; the cap or head of a still</note> with a tube / everything made of glass <note>symbol: ☿; the symbol for Mercury, here referring to the "spirituous" or glass material</note> leading to the receiver / which must be made of glass and be quite large. Place the receiver into a wooden vessel filled with cold water / the receiver must also be covered on top with wet cloths / which are frequently cooled and moistened. In the wooden vessel, there should be a tap / so that one can drain the water / and pour in fresh, cold water again. 

When everything is ready / one pours the prepared spirit of wine <note>original: spiritus vini</note> through the lower holes / filling it just up to the small holes and sets it on fire. Thus the brandy <note>original: Brantwein</note> burns / and the spirit <note>symbol: ☿; the volatile essence</note> is driven upward through the air-holes / and dissolves <note>original: solvirt; here meaning to condense or liquefy</note> because of the cold water / so that it climbs out of the alembic and into the receiver. In this way, the true spirit of wine is prepared. However, you must not fail in the work of cooling at any point / and you must pour in more water of life <note>original: aquam vitæ</note> / so that it does not burn down too low, etc.
